facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: Peter Pan had lived in Neverland for longer than anyone around him could clearly remember or count. He had never aged a single day and his eyes were still as bright and clear as they had ever been. He still crowed with pure delight when he won a fight and still laughed when things went against him. The lost boys around him grew taller each year and eventually left the island one by one for good. But Peter remained exactly and completely the same as he had always been from the very beginning. His secret was not the island's air or Tinker Bell's dust but something that lived entirely inside him. Imagination keeps us young.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: The most remarkable thing about Peter Pan was not that he could fly or fight or crow magnificently. It was that he woke up every single morning as curious and as delighted by the world as he had been the day before. Most people, as they accumulate experience, find that fewer and fewer things genuinely surprise or move them. But Peter approached each new day as if it might contain something he had never encountered or imagined before. This quality — the refusal to let experience become routine — was what the fairy dust was really made of. The lost boys could grow old because they had stopped asking what might happen next with genuine excitement and wonder. Peter could not grow old because he had never stopped asking that question and never intended to stop asking it ever. Imagination keeps us young.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: Peter Pan's permanent youth is usually understood as a fantasy — a wish-fulfillment story about escaping the inevitable. But Barrie's treatment of it suggests something more interesting and more available than simple biological impossibility. The aging that matters most in the story is not physical but imaginative — the gradual dimming of curiosity and wonder. Characters grow old in Barrie's world not when their hair turns grey but when they stop being genuinely surprised by things. Peter's immortality is the immortality of a mind that has never agreed to find the world ordinary and predictable. This form of youth is not available to everyone — it requires a sustained and deliberate refusal to settle into routine. But Barrie suggests it is available to some people across the full span of their lives if they choose it consistently. The imagination that keeps Peter Pan young is the same imagination available to anyone willing to keep exercising it. Imagination keeps us young.
